appraisal_events.evidence: le bourgeoisisme pudibond de l'un, les défauts insupportables de l'autre ne prouvent rien contre eux, puisque leur génie est manifesté par leurs œuvres; de même la prétentieuse vulgarité d'un Elstir à ses débuts ... ce n'est pas le plus spirituel, le plus instruit, le mieux relationné des hommes ... qui devient un Bergotte (les contemporains le tinssent-ils pour moins homme d'esprit que Swann et moins savant que Brichot)
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator repeatedly insists that personal awkwardness, early vulgarity, or a lesser reputation for wit and learning (measured against Swann and Brichot) do not diminish the real stature of Vinteuil, Elstir, and especially Bergotte, since genuine genius is manifested in the work rather than in social brilliance.

appraisal_events.evidence: je sortis ... pour aller voir Mme Verdurin, car elle était, avec Mme Bontemps, une des reines de ce Paris de la guerre qui faisait penser au Directoire.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator names Mme Verdurin and Mme Bontemps as leading 'queens' of wartime Paris society, but the immediately following satirical account of vain, opportunistic war-fashion suggests this elevation carries narratorial irony rather than plain admiration.

status_effects.explanation: Bergotte is elevated as possessing a genius that outstrips contemporaries' surface judgments of his wit and learning.
Vinteuil's off-putting bourgeois primness is dismissed as irrelevant to his manifest genius, though he receives only a passing, parallel mention alongside Bergotte.
Elstir's vulgar, pretentious debut (and his identity as the once-tiresome 'Monsieur Tiche') is framed as a normal stage that geniuses outgrow, culminating in his superior taste.
She is explicitly designated one of the leading social 'queens' of wartime Paris, though the surrounding satire qualifies how admiringly this is meant.
She is named alongside Mme Verdurin as a co-'queen' of wartime Paris society, sharing the same elevated but ironized status.

ambiguities: The elevation built around Bergotte (and, in parallel, Vinteuil and Elstir) rests on a hedged, reflective conditional ('si j'avais compris jadis') rather than a flat assertion, and Swann and Brichot function only as comparative reference points rather than being directly diminished.

The description of Mme Verdurin and Mme Bontemps as 'queens' of wartime Paris is immediately followed by a satirical account of frivolous, self-congratulatory war-fashion, so it is uncertain whether the narrator's framing is admiring or ironic about their social ascendancy.
